meta.titre: Igneous Rock Structures and Textures: reading the cooling history
meta.sous_theme: Textures, intrusive and extrusive structures, and named rocks

sections.contenu_markdown: Mount Cameroon is an active volcano and belongs to the Cameroon Volcanic Line, a chain of volcanic centres, so igneous rocks are part of the landscape of the country. The same molten rock can become a coarse granite deep underground or a fine-grained rhyolite on the surface, and the difference is written in the crystals. At Advanced Level you are asked to name a texture and explain how it formed, to recognise a sill, a dyke or a lava flow in the field, and to describe the composition, texture, rate of cooling and field occurrence of named rocks. Treat texture and structure as a record of where and how fast a magma cooled.

items: Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is magma that has reached the surface.
Minerals crystallise from a melt as it cools, and slow cooling gives the crystals time to grow.
Igneous rocks are grouped by silica content: ultrabasic below about 45 %, basic about 45 to 52 %, intermediate about 52 to 66 % and acid above about 66 %.
Dark minerals such as olivine and pyroxene are rich in iron and magnesium (mafic); light minerals such as quartz and feldspar are felsic.

sections.titre: Textures, intrusive and extrusive structures, and named igneous rocks
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What texture is
**Texture** is the size, shape and arrangement of the crystals (and glass) in a rock. **Structure** is a larger feature of the rock mass: its shape, its contacts and its jointing. Crystal size is controlled mainly by the **rate of cooling**: slow cooling at depth gives few large crystals; rapid cooling at or near the surface gives many tiny crystals or none. Volatile content and the viscosity of the melt also play a part: water-rich melts allow very large crystals to grow.

| Texture | Description | Conditions of formation | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phaneritic | crystals large enough to see without a lens, interlocking | slow cooling, intrusive | granite, gabbro, peridotite |
| Aphanitic | crystals too small to see | rapid cooling, extrusive or shallow | basalt, rhyolite |
| Porphyritic | large crystals (phenocrysts) in a finer groundmass | two stages: slow cooling first, then faster cooling after emplacement or eruption | porphyritic rhyolite or granite |
| Glassy | no crystals | very rapid quenching | obsidian |
| Vesicular | gas holes (vesicles) | gas dissolved in the melt comes out of solution as pressure falls and is trapped when the lava solidifies; vesicles concentrate near the top of a flow | pumice, scoria, vesicular basalt |
| Ophitic | laths of plagioclase enclosed in larger crystals of pyroxene | intermediate cooling in shallow intrusions | dolerite |
| Pegmatitic | exceptionally large crystals | late, water-rich residual melt | pegmatite |
| Pyroclastic | fragments of ash, pumice and crystals, often welded | explosive eruption | tuff, ignimbrite |

When vesicles are later filled by minerals such as calcite or quartz, they are called **amygdales**.

### Describing a texture in an answer
Give the three parts: (1) what you see (grain size, shape, arrangement); (2) the cooling history it implies; (3) the setting (deep intrusion, shallow intrusion or surface flow). Use relative terms accurately: fine, medium and coarse describe the grain size; felsic and mafic describe the mineral composition.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks you to distinguish dykes, sills, batholiths and other intrusions, or to read a cross-cutting relationship.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
An intrusion is **concordant** if it lies parallel to the bedding of the country rock and **discordant** if it cuts across it.

| Body | Form and relation to country rock |
|---|---|
| Batholith | very large, irregular, discordant mass with an outcrop of more than 100 km squared, usually granitic |
| Stock | like a batholith but with an outcrop of less than 100 km squared |
| Dyke | thin sheet, often vertical or steep, discordant, cutting across the bedding |
| Sill | thin sheet, often horizontal in horizontal beds, concordant, lying between the beds |
| Laccolith | concordant lens with a flat base and a domed top that lifts the beds above |
| Volcanic neck | solidified magma filling the feeder pipe of a volcano |

Evidence of intrusion: a **chilled margin** (finer grain at the edge of the body where it cooled quickly against cold country rock), **baked contacts** (contact metamorphism of the country rock) and **xenoliths** (fragments of country rock inside the igneous body). A dyke is **younger** than the rocks it cuts. A sill bakes the beds both above and below it; a lava flow bakes only the beds beneath it, and has a vesicular, weathered or reddened top covered by later sediment.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question describes volcanic features or asks about the form of lava and pyroclastic deposits.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
- **Lava flows:** sheets of lava; basalt lava is runny and spreads far, while viscous acid lava piles up as **lava domes**. A flow often has a vesicular top.
- **Columnar jointing:** contraction on cooling splits a thick flow or sheet into polygonal columns, often six-sided, set at right angles to the cooling surface.
- **Pillow lava:** lava erupted under water forms rounded pillows with glassy rims.
- **Pyroclastic deposits:** ash, pumice and fragments thrown out explosively; tuff is consolidated ash, and **ignimbrite** is a welded deposit from a hot pyroclastic flow.
- **Volcanoes:** shield volcanoes (runny basalt, gentle slopes), composite volcanoes (alternating lava and ash, more viscous lava, explosive eruptions) and cinder cones; a caldera is a large depression formed when a volcano collapses.

Viscosity increases with silica content, so acid magmas tend to erupt explosively and basic magmas tend to flow.

variantes.nom: Composition, texture and occurrence of named rocks
variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must discuss rocks such as peridotite, dolerite and rhyolite under the headings composition, texture, rate of cooling and field occurrence.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Rock | Composition | Texture | Cooling | Field occurrence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peridotite | ultramafic (silica below about 45 %): olivine with pyroxene; dark and dense | coarse, phaneritic | very slow, deep | large layered intrusions, ultramafic bodies, ophiolites, xenoliths in basalt |
| Dolerite | basic (mafic): plagioclase and pyroxene (augite) | medium-grained, often ophitic | intermediate, shallow | dykes and sills |
| Rhyolite | acid (felsic): quartz, alkali feldspar and some mica; pale | fine-grained or glassy, often porphyritic, may show flow banding | rapid, at the surface | lava flows and domes, and ignimbrite sheets at explosive continental volcanoes |

Related pairs: basalt (extrusive) and gabbro (intrusive) have the same composition; rhyolite (extrusive) and granite (intrusive) have the same composition. Only the cooling history, and therefore the texture, differs.

sections.enonce_markdown: In a quarry, a sheet of dark rock lies between layers of sandstone that dip at 30 degrees. The sheet is medium-grained and consists of laths of plagioclase enclosed in larger crystals of pyroxene. The sandstone is baked and hardened both above and below it, and the edges of the sheet are finer-grained than its centre. On a level quarry floor, the outcrop width of the sheet, measured at right angles to the strike, is 40 m. (a) Name the rock and the texture. (b) State whether the sheet is a sill or a lava flow, giving reasons. (c) Calculate its true thickness. (d) Explain why the margins are finer than the centre.

etapes.action: Identify the rock and the texture.
etapes.justification: Plagioclase laths inside pyroxene crystals is the ophitic texture, and a dark, medium-grained basic rock with it is dolerite.

etapes.action: Decide between an intrusion and a lava flow.
etapes.justification: A lava flow bakes only the rock beneath it, whereas an intrusion heats the rock on both sides. Sandstone baked above and below, and finer edges (chilled margins), show intrusion.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The sheet was emplaced after the sandstones; because it lies between the beds, it is concordant: a **sill**.

etapes.action: Write the formula for true thickness.
etapes.justification: The outcrop on level ground is a slanting cut across a sheet that dips; the true thickness is the perpendicular distance between the contacts.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $t = w \sin\delta$, where $w$ is the outcrop width and $\delta$ the dip

etapes.justification: The width is measured at right angles to the strike, which is the condition for the formula.
Crystal size depends on the rate of cooling.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The margins lost heat quickly to the cold sandstone and formed a chilled margin of small crystals; the centre stayed hot longer and cooled slowly, giving larger crystals.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The rock is **dolerite** with **ophitic** texture and the body is a **sill** with a true thickness of **20 m**. The finer edges are chilled margins formed by rapid cooling against cold country rock, while the slower-cooling centre is coarser.

items.erreur_markdown: A porphyritic rock is one that is coarse-grained throughout, or one full of gas holes.
items.pourquoi_faux: Porphyritic texture is a mixture: large crystals (phenocrysts) set in a much finer groundmass. Gas holes make a vesicular texture.
items.correction_markdown: Porphyritic = **large phenocrysts in a fine groundmass**, showing two stages of cooling.

items.erreur_markdown: A sill cuts across the bedding, while a dyke lies parallel to it.
items.pourquoi_faux: The terms are reversed. A dyke is discordant; a sill is concordant.
items.correction_markdown: **Dyke:** discordant, cuts across the bedding. **Sill:** concordant, lies parallel to the bedding.

items.erreur_markdown: Rapid cooling of magma gives large crystals.
items.pourquoi_faux: Large crystals need time to grow. Rapid cooling leaves little time and gives many small crystals or glass.
items.correction_markdown: **Slow cooling gives large crystals**; **rapid cooling gives small crystals or glass**.

items.erreur_markdown: Vesicles are holes made later by weathering and dissolving of the rock.
items.pourquoi_faux: Vesicles are formed while the lava is still liquid: dissolved gases come out of solution as pressure falls and the bubbles are trapped when the lava solidifies.
items.correction_markdown: Vesicles are **gas bubbles frozen into lava**, mainly near the top of the flow; when filled later by minerals they are called amygdales.

items.erreur_markdown: Rhyolite is an intrusive rock because it contains quartz and feldspar like granite.
items.pourquoi_faux: Rhyolite has the same composition as granite but is extrusive and fine-grained, because it cooled quickly at the surface.
items.correction_markdown: **Granite** is intrusive, coarse-grained; **rhyolite** is extrusive, fine-grained, with the same acid composition.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the igneous texture described in each case. (a) Interlocking crystals large enough to see without a lens. (b) A glassy rock with no crystals. (c) Large crystals set in a fine-grained groundmass. (d) A rock full of small cavities left by gas.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Phaneritic** (coarse-grained, slow cooling at depth).

(b) **Glassy** (obsidian, very rapid quenching).

(c) **Porphyritic** (two stages of cooling).

(d) **Vesicular** (gas bubbles trapped in lava).

items.enonce_markdown: (a) A granite intrusion cuts across folded sedimentary beds, and its outcrop is approximately a rectangle 12 km by 10 km. A second granite outcrop 3 km by 4 km cuts across the same beds. Name the two bodies, using the area as the test. (b) A sheet of dolerite dips at 45 degrees. On level ground its outcrop is 30 m wide, measured at right angles to the strike. Calculate the true thickness.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) First outcrop: $12 \times 10 = 120\ \mathrm{km^2}$, which is more than $100\ \mathrm{km^2}$ and is discordant: a **batholith**. Second outcrop: $3 \times 4 = 12\ \mathrm{km^2}$, less than $100\ \mathrm{km^2}$: a **stock**.

(b) $t = w\sin\delta = 30 \times \sin 45^\circ = 30 \times 0.7071 = 21.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

**120 km squared: batholith; 12 km squared: stock; true thickness of the sheet 21 m (21.2 m).**

items.enonce_markdown: Granite and rhyolite have the same mineral composition. (a) Explain why their textures differ. (b) Describe how a porphyritic texture forms in a lava. (c) Explain why vesicles are concentrated near the top of a basalt lava flow and why a thick basalt flow may develop columnar joints.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Granite cooled slowly deep in the crust, so crystals had time to grow and form a coarse, phaneritic rock. Rhyolite cooled quickly at or near the surface, so it is fine-grained (aphanitic) or glassy.

(b) The magma begins to cool slowly in a chamber, and a few large crystals (phenocrysts) grow. The magma, with its crystals, is then erupted or intruded to a shallow level, where the remaining liquid cools quickly and forms a fine groundmass around the earlier crystals. The rock therefore shows two stages of cooling.

(c) Gas that was dissolved in the magma comes out of solution as the lava loses pressure; the bubbles rise, and the lava solidifies from the surface downward, so the gas is trapped in the upper part as vesicles. Contraction as the lava cools produces tensional cracks that run from the cooling surface inward and divide the flow into polygonal, often six-sided, columns.

**Same composition, different cooling rate: slow gives granite, fast gives rhyolite; porphyritic = slow then fast.**

items_markdown: Texture records cooling: slow cooling at depth gives large crystals (phaneritic), rapid cooling near or at the surface gives small crystals (aphanitic) or glass; porphyritic means two stages of cooling.
Vesicles are gas bubbles trapped in lava as dissolved gas comes out of solution; they are concentrated near the top of a flow.
A dyke is discordant, a sill is concordant, a batholith is a very large discordant body (outcrop above 100 km squared), a stock is smaller; a laccolith is concordant with a domed top.
Intrusion evidence: chilled margins, baked contacts on both sides of a sill, xenoliths; a lava flow bakes only the beds beneath it and may have a vesicular, weathered top.

Peridotite: ultramafic, olivine and pyroxene, coarse, very slow cooling; dolerite: basic, plagioclase and pyroxene, medium-grained, ophitic, in dykes and sills; rhyolite: acid, quartz and feldspar, fine-grained or glassy, in lavas, domes and ignimbrites.
True thickness of a dipping sheet on level ground: $t = w \sin\delta$, with $w$ measured at right angles to the strike.
